lit: the tan flower appears once: a bloom seen only briefly and rarely

story.text: The phrase goes back to the Lotus Sutra. The Buddha tells his disciple Shariputra that the buddhas teach this wonderful dharma only rarely, just as the udumbara flower (tan hua for short) appears only once in a very long time. Later the name came to be associated with the night-blooming cereus, whose flower opens for a few hours and then withers, and the phrase came to mean something brilliant that vanishes quickly.

use.how: Predicate or after 是/只是/不过是, about fame, success, a trend or a talent that shone and then faded: 他的走红只是昙花一现。

near.diff: 过眼云烟 says something passes and is not worth caring about; 昙花一现 stresses that a success or splendour was real but very short.

cue: A singer had one viral hit, topped the charts for a month, and then disappeared from public view. How would you describe her fame?

ctx.s: 这家网红店火了一个月就关门了，真是{昙花一现}。
ctx.en: That trendy shop was the rage for a month and then closed down; its success didn't last at all.

ctx.s: 很多选秀歌手只是{昙花一现}，几年后就没人记得了。
ctx.en: Many talent-show singers are only a flash in the pan; a few years later nobody remembers them.

ctx.s: 他这次考了第一，你觉得会不会只是{昙花一现}？
ctx.en: He came first this time; do you think it might just be a one-off?

ctx.s: “这股热潮会持续吗？”“我看不过是{昙花一现}。”
ctx.en: "Will this craze last?" "I think it's just a passing flash."

ctx.s: 那位作家的成名作轰动一时，此后却再无佳作，他的辉煌如{昙花一现}。
ctx.en: That writer's breakthrough book caused a sensation, but nothing good followed; his glory was brief.

ctx.s: 要让改革的成果不至于{昙花一现}，关键在于建立长期机制。
ctx.en: To keep the results of the reform from being short-lived, the key is to build long-term mechanisms.

bad.s: 今天的会议{昙花一现}，只开了十分钟。
bad.en: (meant: today's meeting was very short, only ten minutes)
bad.why: It is about success or splendour that fades fast, not about an event simply being short.

bad.s: 这家老店开了一百年，生意一直{昙花一现}。
bad.en: (meant: this old shop has flourished for a hundred years)
bad.why: It means a brief glory that fades at once, so it cannot describe success that has lasted a century.

mean: the place is the same but the people are gone
lit: things are as they were, people are not

story.text: The phrase is best known from a lyric by the Song poet Li Qingzhao, written in her later years after her husband had died and she had fled south. After the wind has dropped and the blossoms have fallen, she writes: the things remain, the people have changed, everything is over; I want to speak, but tears come first.

use.how: Said with a sigh, as a comment or after 真是/已, when a familiar place or object remains but the people who belonged to it are gone or changed.

near.diff: 沧海桑田 is about the world itself changing completely over a long time; 物是人非 says the place stays and only the people are gone.

cue: You return to your old school after twenty years: the buildings are exactly the same, but none of the people you knew are there.

ctx.s: 回到小时候住的院子，邻居都搬走了，真是{物是人非}。
ctx.en: I went back to the courtyard where I lived as a child; the neighbours have all moved away. Nothing has changed but the people.

ctx.s: 母校的教学楼还在，老师们却都退休了，{物是人非}啊。
ctx.en: My old school's buildings are still there, but the teachers have all retired. The place is the same, the people are gone.

ctx.s: 奶奶去世后再回老家，院子里那棵树还在，却已{物是人非}。
ctx.en: Going back home after Grandma died, the tree in the yard was still there, but she was not.

ctx.s: “你还去那家咖啡馆吗？”“不去了，{物是人非}，去了只会难过。”
ctx.en: "Do you still go to that café?" "No. It's the same place, but the people are gone; going would just make me sad."

ctx.s: 他翻看着十年前的合影，照片里的地方都还在，人却散了，不禁感慨{物是人非}。
ctx.en: Looking through a group photo from ten years ago, he saw the places were all still there but the people had scattered, and he sighed at how things had changed.

ctx.s: 小说结尾，主人公重返故乡，心中满是{物是人非}的感慨。
ctx.en: At the end of the novel the hero returns home, full of sorrow that the place remains while the people are gone.

bad.s: 新公司装修得很漂亮，跟以前完全不一样，真是{物是人非}。
bad.en: (meant: the new office looks completely different)
bad.why: It needs the place to stay the same while the people are gone; here the place itself changed and nobody is missing.

bad.s: 他换了个新发型，我差点认不出来，真是{物是人非}。
bad.en: (meant: he looks so different)
bad.why: It is a wistful sigh about lost people and times, not a remark on someone's changed appearance.

mean: (of a task or problem) so pressing it cannot wait a moment
lit: not even a moment allows delay

use.how: Predicate after a task or action, or before 的事: 抢修工作刻不容缓。 Said of what must be done; not used for a person acting hastily.

near.diff: 当务之急 is a noun naming the most urgent task (当务之急是…); 刻不容缓 is a predicate saying a task cannot wait.
迫在眉睫 pictures a danger or need already right before one's eyes; 刻不容缓 says the action must not be put off even a moment.

cue: A dam above a town is cracking, and engineers warn that any delay could be fatal. How urgent is the repair work?

ctx.s: 病人大出血，手术{刻不容缓}。
ctx.en: The patient is haemorrhaging; the operation cannot wait a moment.

ctx.s: 河堤出现了裂缝，抢修工作{刻不容缓}，一分钟也不能耽误。
ctx.en: Cracks have appeared in the dyke; the emergency repairs must start at once, without losing a single minute.

ctx.s: 服务器被攻击了，修补漏洞{刻不容缓}。
ctx.en: The server has been attacked; patching the hole can't wait.

ctx.s: “这件事能不能等到下周？”“不能，这是{刻不容缓}的事。”
ctx.en: "Can this wait until next week?" "No, this has to be done right now."

ctx.s: 时间就是生命，救人{刻不容缓}，搜救队连夜出发了。
ctx.en: Every second counts: rescuing people couldn't wait a moment, so the search team set off that very night.

ctx.s: 灾区急需饮用水，救援物资的运送{刻不容缓}。
ctx.en: The disaster area urgently needs drinking water; getting relief supplies there cannot wait.

bad.s: 他饿坏了，{刻不容缓}地吃完了一大碗面。
bad.en: (meant: he was starving and wolfed down a big bowl of noodles)
bad.why: It describes a task that must not be delayed, not a person doing something eagerly or hurriedly.

bad.s: 这件事{刻不容缓}，我们下个月再讨论吧。
bad.en: (meant: this matter is important, let's discuss it next month)
bad.why: Saying something cannot wait a moment and then postponing it to next month contradicts the idiom.

lit: the urgent one among the tasks at hand

story.text: Mencius said that the wise know everything, yet treat the tasks that matter most at the present moment as the urgent ones; and the benevolent love everyone, yet put first the urgent work of being close to worthy people. Even a sage, he argued, cannot do all things at once and must choose what comes first.

use.how: A noun phrase, usually as subject in 当务之急是…, or after 是/才是: 现在的当务之急是找到资金。

near.diff: 刻不容缓 is a predicate (这件事刻不容缓); 当务之急 is a noun naming which task comes first (当务之急是…).

cue: Your startup has a dozen problems, but paying this month's salaries must be dealt with before any of them. Name that task.

ctx.s: 刚搬进新家，{当务之急}是把网络装好。
ctx.en: We've just moved in; the first thing to sort out is the internet.

ctx.s: 公司现金流快断了，{当务之急}是先找到资金。
ctx.en: The company is about to run out of cash; the most urgent thing is to find money.

ctx.s: 你现在的{当务之急}不是玩游戏，而是准备下周的考试。
ctx.en: Your priority right now isn't gaming, it's preparing for next week's exam.

ctx.s: “我们该先做什么？”“{当务之急}是联系上孩子的家长。”
ctx.en: "What should we do first?" "The most urgent thing is to get hold of the child's parents."

ctx.s: 对这座老城来说，修复排水系统才是{当务之急}。
ctx.en: For this old city, repairing the drainage system is what matters most right now.

ctx.s: 他意识到，比起换工作，把身体养好才是自己的{当务之急}。
ctx.en: He realised that, more than changing jobs, getting his health back was his real priority.

bad.s: 这件事很{当务之急}，你快去办吧。
bad.en: (meant: this is very urgent, go and do it)
bad.why: It is a noun, not an adjective, so it cannot take hen; say the matter is urgent (hen ji), or call it the top priority with shi.

bad.s: 十年后买一套大房子是我的{当务之急}。
bad.en: (meant: buying a big house in ten years is my main goal)
bad.why: It means the most pressing task right now, so it cannot name a goal ten years away.

lit: pressed so that one cannot stop

use.how: Adverbial before a verb (迫不得已才…), or as predicate (是迫不得已的). Often used to justify an unwelcome choice someone had no way to avoid.

near.diff: 迫不及待 means too eager to wait; 迫不得已 means forced against one's wishes. They look alike but are near opposites in feeling.
身不由己 is an ongoing state of not being one's own master; 迫不得已 is about one particular choice forced by circumstances.

cue: The last train has gone and you hate spending money, but you have no other way home than an expensive taxi. Explain why you took it.

ctx.s: 末班车走了，我{迫不得已}打车回家。
ctx.en: The last bus had gone, so I had no choice but to take a taxi home.

ctx.s: 要不是{迫不得已}，谁愿意离开家乡去外地打工？
ctx.en: Who would leave home to work far away unless they had to?

ctx.s: 房租涨得太厉害，老板{迫不得已}才关了这家餐厅。
ctx.en: The rent went up so much that the owner was forced to close the restaurant.

ctx.s: “你为什么卖掉那辆车？”“{迫不得已}，家里急需用钱。”
ctx.en: "Why did you sell that car?" "I had no choice; the family needed money urgently."

ctx.s: 这么做实在是{迫不得已}，希望大家理解。
ctx.en: We really had no alternative; we hope everyone understands.

ctx.s: 由于暴雨，主办方{迫不得已}将演唱会改到下个月。
ctx.en: Because of the rainstorm, the organisers were forced to move the concert to next month.

bad.s: 放假了，我{迫不得已}想见到你。
bad.en: (meant: now it's the holidays, I can't wait to see you)
bad.why: Being too eager to wait is po bu ji dai; po bu de yi means doing something against one's will.

bad.s: 这家的饺子太好吃了，我{迫不得已}吃了三盘。
bad.en: (meant: the dumplings were so good I couldn't help eating three plates)
bad.why: Not being able to resist something pleasant is ren bu zhu; this idiom means being forced by bad circumstances.

mean: not in control of one's own actions
lit: the body does not follow oneself

use.how: Predicate or adverbial (身不由己地…). Said when a role, job, situation or physical force decides what one does; often as an excuse: 人在江湖，身不由己。

near.diff: 迫不得已 is one forced choice at one moment; 身不由己 describes a situation where one is not one's own master at all.

cue: Your job keeps forcing you into things you don't want to do, like drinking at business dinners. How do you describe your position?

ctx.s: 地铁里人太多，我被挤得{身不由己}，一直往后退。
ctx.en: The metro was so packed that I was pushed backwards and couldn't stop myself.

ctx.s: 他也不想天天加班，可在这个岗位上{身不由己}。
ctx.en: He doesn't want to work late every day either, but in that position he has no say.

ctx.s: “你怎么又喝醉了？”“应酬嘛，{身不由己}。”
ctx.en: "Drunk again?" "Business dinners. It's not up to me."

ctx.s: 当上经理以后，她常常感到{身不由己}，连休假都要看公司安排。
ctx.en: Since becoming a manager she often feels she isn't her own master; even her holidays depend on the company.

ctx.s: 电影里的卧底警察说：“我做的很多事都是{身不由己}。”
ctx.en: The undercover cop in the film says, "Much of what I did, I had no control over."

ctx.s: 那段日子，他被卷进家族的纷争，{身不由己}地站到了父亲那边。
ctx.en: In those days he was dragged into the family feud and found himself, against his will, on his father's side.

bad.s: 今天没有安排，我{身不由己}，想去哪儿就去哪儿。
bad.en: (meant: I'm free today and can go wherever I like)
bad.why: It means the opposite: not being free to decide what one does.

bad.s: 我发烧了，全身{身不由己}，很难受。
bad.en: (meant: I have a fever and feel awful all over)
bad.why: It is about one's actions being controlled by circumstances, not about feeling physically unwell.

lit: following the heart in whatever it wants

story.text: The idiom is traced to Confucius's summary of his own life in the Analects: at fifteen he set his heart on learning, at thirty he stood firm, and so on, until at seventy he could follow what his heart desired without overstepping the rules. The modern idiom keeps the first half, following the heart, and drops the rule-keeping.

use.how: Adverbial (随心所欲地…) or predicate. Freedom to act as one likes; neutral or positive, and negative only after 不能/别: 钱不能随心所欲地花。

near.diff: 为所欲为 is always condemnation of doing wrong without restraint; 随心所欲 is just freedom to act as one likes, often a good thing.

cue: It's the first day of the holidays: no alarm, no schedule, and you can do whatever you feel like all day.

ctx.s: 放假了，终于可以{随心所欲}地睡懒觉。
ctx.en: The holidays are here; at last I can sleep in as much as I like.

ctx.s: 这款软件可以让你{随心所欲}地调整页面布局。
ctx.en: This software lets you adjust the page layout however you like.

ctx.s: “旅行要不要做计划？”“我喜欢{随心所欲}，走到哪儿算哪儿。”
ctx.en: "Do you plan your trips?" "I like to go wherever I feel like and see where I end up."

ctx.s: 钱不是大风刮来的，你不能这样{随心所欲}地花。
ctx.en: Money doesn't grow on trees; you can't just spend it however you please.

ctx.s: 写初稿时可以{随心所欲}，修改时再讲究结构。
ctx.en: In a first draft you can write freely; worry about structure when you revise.

ctx.s: 他的书法已到了{随心所欲}的境界，每一笔都自然而有分寸。
ctx.en: His calligraphy has reached the stage where he writes freely, every stroke natural yet controlled.

bad.s: “我们去哪家餐厅？”“{随心所欲}！”
bad.en: (meant: "Which restaurant?" "Whatever you like!")
bad.why: It describes how someone acts, not a reply handing the choice to the other person; say sui ni or ting ni de.

bad.s: 他这次考试{随心所欲}，考了满分。
bad.en: (meant: the exam went just as he hoped and he got full marks)
bad.why: It means acting freely, not results turning out as hoped; for that say ru yuan yi chang or xin xiang shi cheng.

mean: to do whatever one likes, however wrong
lit: to do whatever one wishes to do

use.how: Intransitive predicate, often after 可以/敢/不能: 别以为有钱就可以为所欲为。 Condemns someone, usually with money or power, who ignores rules and others.

near.diff: 随心所欲 is neutral freedom to do as one likes; 为所欲为 condemns doing wrong because nothing stops one.
肆无忌惮 stresses brazenness and usually modifies a specific act (肆无忌惮地…); 为所欲为 says someone does whatever they like.

cue: The boss's nephew ignores every company rule, bullies staff and takes what he wants, and nobody dares to stop him.

ctx.s: 别以为有钱就可以{为所欲为}。
ctx.en: Don't think that having money means you can do whatever you want.

ctx.s: 那个经理仗着老板是他舅舅，在公司里{为所欲为}。
ctx.en: That manager, relying on the boss being his uncle, does whatever he likes in the company.

ctx.s: “他凭什么想罚款就罚款？”“没人管他，他当然敢{为所欲为}。”
ctx.en: "What right does he have to fine people whenever he likes?" "Nobody keeps him in check, so of course he does as he pleases."

ctx.s: 法律的存在，就是为了不让任何人{为所欲为}。
ctx.en: Laws exist precisely so that no one can do whatever they like.

ctx.s: 这个小区的物业缺少监督，长期{为所欲为}，业主怨声载道。
ctx.en: The estate's management company has no oversight and has done as it pleased for years; the residents are furious.

ctx.s: 故事里的恶霸在镇上{为所欲为}，直到新县令到任。
ctx.en: In the story the local bully did whatever he wanted in the town until the new magistrate arrived.

bad.s: 老师鼓励我们{为所欲为}，大胆发挥创造力。
bad.en: (meant: the teacher encouraged us to be free and creative)
bad.why: It always condemns wrongdoing, so no teacher would encourage it; say zi you fa hui or sui xin suo yu.

bad.s: 他{为所欲为}了这家公司。
bad.en: (meant: he did whatever he wanted with this company)
bad.why: It takes no object; put the place before it with zai: he does as he likes in the company.

lit: unbridled, with nothing feared or held back

use.how: Mostly adverbial before a specific act (肆无忌惮地骂人/排污), sometimes predicate. Condemns behaviour done openly with no regard for rules or others.

near.diff: 为所欲为 says someone does whatever they like in general; 肆无忌惮 stresses the brazen, open manner of a particular act.

cue: In a quiet library, a man shouts into his phone for twenty minutes, ignoring the glares of everyone around him.

ctx.s: 他在图书馆里{肆无忌惮}地大声打电话。
ctx.en: He was talking loudly on the phone in the library without the slightest regard for anyone.

ctx.s: 有些网友躲在屏幕后面，{肆无忌惮}地辱骂别人。
ctx.en: Some people hide behind their screens and insult others with complete brazenness.

ctx.s: 这家工厂{肆无忌惮}地往河里排放污水。
ctx.en: This factory openly dumps waste water into the river without any scruple.

ctx.s: 小偷竟然在大白天{肆无忌惮}地撬车门。
ctx.en: The thief brazenly forced car doors open in broad daylight.

ctx.s: “他怎么敢这样跟老师说话？”“仗着他爸是校长，越来越{肆无忌惮}了。”
ctx.en: "How dare he talk to the teacher like that?" "His dad's the head, so he's getting more and more brazen."

ctx.s: 文章批评了某些商家{肆无忌惮}地夸大宣传、欺骗消费者的做法。
ctx.en: The article criticised some businesses for shamelessly exaggerating their claims and deceiving consumers.

bad.s: 他{肆无忌惮}地努力学习，每天学到半夜。
bad.en: (meant: he studied with total dedication until midnight)
bad.why: It condemns brazen wrongdoing; it cannot describe hard work.

bad.s: 消防员{肆无忌惮}地冲进火场救人。
bad.en: (meant: the firefighters fearlessly rushed into the fire)
bad.why: Fearless courage deserves praise, such as fen bu gu shen; this idiom means flouting rules and would insult them.

mean: with no turning back, for what one knows is right

story.text: The wording goes back to the Han writer Sima Xiangru's proclamation to the people of Ba and Shu. He praised the men of the border regions who, at the first alarm, took up their bows and ran to fight, facing bare blades and flying arrows: duty would not let them look back, nor their resolve let them turn on their heels. His wording was yi bu fan gu; the bu (not) later became wu (no).

use.how: Mostly adverbial (义无反顾地…) before a committed act: going, joining, standing up. Praises someone who goes ahead for a just cause despite cost or danger.

near.diff: 一意孤行 criticises stubbornly going one's own way against advice; 义无反顾 praises going ahead because it is right.

cue: Knowing she will lose her well-paid job, a nurse still volunteers for a dangerous rescue mission because it is the right thing to do.

ctx.s: 听说家乡发生地震，他{义无反顾}地回去当志愿者。
ctx.en: Hearing of the earthquake in his hometown, he went straight back to volunteer without a second thought.

ctx.s: 她放弃了高薪工作，{义无反顾}地投身乡村教育。
ctx.en: She gave up a well-paid job and devoted herself to rural education without looking back.

ctx.s: “你想清楚了吗？”“想清楚了，这条路我会{义无反顾}地走下去。”
ctx.en: "Have you thought it through?" "I have. I'll follow this path to the end, whatever it costs."

ctx.s: 明知揭发真相会丢掉工作，他还是{义无反顾}地站了出来。
ctx.en: He knew exposing the truth would cost him his job, yet he stood up without hesitation.

ctx.s: 疫情最严重的时候，许多医生{义无反顾}地奔赴一线。
ctx.en: At the worst of the epidemic, many doctors went resolutely to the front line.

ctx.s: 小说中的主人公为了救出朋友，{义无反顾}地冲进了燃烧的大楼。
ctx.en: In the novel, the hero rushes into the burning building without hesitation to save his friend.

bad.s: 他输光了钱，还是{义无反顾}地去赌博。
bad.en: (meant: even after losing everything, he still went on gambling)
bad.why: It praises resolve for a just cause; for persisting in a vice say zhi mi bu wu or lu jiao bu gai.

bad.s: 他{义无反顾}地往前走，没听见我在后面叫他。
bad.en: (meant: he walked on without looking back and didn't hear me calling)
bad.why: Looking back here means moral hesitation, not literally turning round; it is not about walking on without looking behind.
